newsitem.title: NORWAY: Nobel committee stirs controvery with peace prize.
newsitem.headline: Nobel committee stirs controvery with peace prize.

text.p: The Norwegian Nobel Committee has again stirred political controversy by awarding the 1996 Peace Prize to two East Timor campaigners in full realisation that the decision could antagonise Indonesia which rules the territory.

Committee chairman Francis Sejersted made his point clearly on Friday after announcing that the prize would go to East Timor Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo and resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta.
"We do hope there is a message (in this award)...to the Indonesian government to change its policy," he told reporters at the Nobel Institute.
Sejersted said the award could trigger a negative response from Jakarta. "We do hope the reaction will be positive but of course we do recognise it could be negative," he said.
"This was about to become a forgotten conflict and we wanted to contribute to maintaining the momentum," Sejersted said.

In late 1975 Indonesian troops invaded the eastern half of Timor island after the Portuguese colonial rulers of 400 years pulled out, annexing the territory that lies in the Indonesian archipegalo, about 500 kms (300 miles) north of Australia.
The United Nations still does not recognise the annexation.
"It can be argued that this is an hour of destiny. You can today see both the possibility of a peaceful solution but there is also the possibility of it going another direction."

The Nobel committee said in a statement an estimated one third of the people of East Timor had died due to starvation, epidemics, war and terror in the 21 years of Indonesian oppression. The population currently stands at about 800,000.
"The Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to honour (Belo's and Ramos-Horta's) sustained and self-sacrificing contributions for a small but oppressed people," the committee said.
Indonesia's instant reaction was one of surprise.
"I don't understand what were the criteria by which they chose them," State Secretary Murdiono told reporters.
The 1996 award was by no means the Norwegian committee's first foray into controversy -- and previous awards have proved the award is no guarantee of political success.

Past Nobel Peace laureates include Burma's opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi (1991), who was only finally released from house arrest in Rangoon after six years last year, and the Dalai Lama (1989), Tibet's spiritual and political leader, whose remote Himalayan state remains at loggerheads with China.

The award, first given in 1901 by a foundation set up by Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel, has frequently gone to politicians in the middle of a peace process or little known activists with the clear aim of boosting their cause.

In 1993 the award went jointly to Nelson Mandela and South African president F. W. de Klerk and in 1994 the winners were then Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, since assassinated, Foreign Minister Shimon Peres and PLO chairman Yasser Arafat.
"This is fundamently a political prize so that is what the whole thing is about," Sejersted said.
Norway's foreign minister, Bjorn Tore Godal, gave his backing to the t was controversial but hoping it could break the current deadlock in East Timor.
"To my mind the more controversial (Nobel) prizes have been among the more interesting ones," Godal told reporters.

"We definitely take a positive view vis-a-vis today's award. We see it as support to the negotiating efforts and the important work of the Nobel Peace winners in order to have a non-violent solution to the remaining problems in East Timor."
